# FINAL EXPERIMENT DESIGN — Directional Retrieval Bias in LLM Factual Recall of Celebrity Parent–Child Relations

**Status:** Design document only. No experiment was executed; no results are claimed. The only computations performed during design were (a) workspace inspection and (b) a Monte-Carlo power simulation to justify sample size (reported in §5). Everything else below is a specification for future execution.

---

## 1. Research question and hypothesis

**H1 (directional bias):** When queried about a real-world celebrity parent–child relationship, LLMs retrieve the **parent given the child** (child→parent, "forward") more accurately than the **child given the parent** (parent→child, "reverse"), measured within the same entity pair.

**H0:** Direction has no effect on accuracy for a fixed factual triple.

**Secondary hypotheses:**
- H2: The reverse-direction deficit manifests disproportionately as *confabulation* (a confidently returned wrong child) rather than *abstention* ("I don't know"), because autoregressive completion of "X's child is ___" plausibly continues toward some plausible name.
- H3 (scale): the direction gap shrinks with model scale (tested within one model family at multiple sizes).

---

## 2. Task set construction

### 2.1 Source and unit
- **Ground truth:** Wikipedia/Wikidata-sourced parent–child relations ("child" / "parent" / "father" / "mother" property statements), cross-checked against a second source (e.g., reputable biography or entertainment reference) for each included pair.
- **Unit of analysis:** one entity triple (Parent P, Child C, relation type), where **both P and C are individually Wikipedia-notable** with standalone articles. The famous-parent/less-notable-child case is **not excluded**; it forms one explicit salience stratification cell (§2.4).

### 2.2 Adjudication rule for blended/adoptive families (stated convention)
- **Primary dataset (default): biological relations only.** Include a pair only if the biological (or, for gestational surrogacy cases, the documented biological link) parent–child relation is stated in both sources. Adoptive and step relations are excluded from the primary set.
- **Robustness set:** a small supplementary subset (~30 pairs) of well-documented adoptive/step relations, analyzed separately and never pooled with the primary set. This isolates whether the direction effect differs for relations likely phrased differently in training text.

### 2.3 Ambiguity and name handling
- **Prompt-side uniqueness:** each probe names exactly one entity. A pair is excluded from the primary set if the prompt-side name collides with (a) another celebrity of comparable or higher salience with the same name, or (b) any entity plausibly confusable in the family domain. Disambiguating role hints ("the American actor…") are used uniformly in both directions, so hints do not differentially favor one direction.
- **Answer-side alias table:** for scoring, each entity has a canonical name plus an alias set (stage names, full legal names, common misspellings, e.g., "Coco" Arquette). The alias table is built once, blind to model outputs, from the same sources as ground truth.
- **Counterbalanced relation wording:** each pair appears in two template variants — gendered (mother/father, son/daughter, matched to the true relation) and neutral ("parent", "child") — counterbalanced for order, so wording asymmetry cannot masquerade as direction asymmetry.

### 2.4 Salience stratification (difficulty balancing between directions)
Each entity gets a salience score S (primary proxy: mean log10 Wikipedia pageviews over a fixed 12-month window; fallback proxy: article length percentile, pre-specified in case pageview data cannot be obtained offline). For each pair, record S_prompt(entity being asked about) and S_answer(target entity). Stratify pairs into 3 cells:
1. High–High (both endpoints S in top tercile)
2. Mixed (one endpoint top tercile, one bottom tercile) — this cell is further split by *which* endpoint is famous, giving four direction-salience combinations
3. Low–Low / famous-parent-obscure-child cell (includes the researcher-sanctioned famous-parent/notable-but-lesser-known-child case, kept as a labeled cell rather than excluded)

**Critical balance constraint:** within each salience cell, the distribution of S for the *prompt-side* entity must be matched across the two directions. That is, when comparing "who is C's parent" vs. "who is P's child," the entity named in the question is matched on salience across directions by construction (it is literally the same entity in the pair), and the *target-side* salience is recorded as a covariate so that "easier-to-name target" cannot confound the direction effect.

### 2.5 Contamination / cutoff policy (stated convention)
- **Inclusion rule:** every included pair must be verifiable in sources dated **before 2022-01-01**, which predates the training cutoff of every model in the panel. This makes the whole primary set "likely-in-training" and removes date as a confound between models.
- **Secondary stratification:** record for each pair a "reference density" indicator (number of pre-2022 sources stating the relation: 1 vs. ≥3). Pairs stated in only one marginal source are flagged *borderline* and analyzed as a stratum. No post-cutoff facts are included, so no unfair negatives exist.
- Note: both directions of a given fact typically co-occur in the same source documents; co-occurrence is thus constant within pair by design — the test isolates *retrieval direction*, not training-data presence.

### 2.6 Size
Target **N = 200 primary pairs** (acceptable operating range 150–300), allocated roughly evenly across salience cells. Justification in §5.

---

## 3. Model panel

All models evaluated zero-shot, greedy decoding (temperature 0), identical system prompt, max completion length 64 tokens. Panel (as specified by the researcher; named here as concrete exemplars of each class — final names may be swapped for whatever is available at execution time, with the class structure preserved):

| Slot | Exemplar | Role |
|---|---|---|
| Small | Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct | base of scale curve |
| Family ladder | Llama-3.1-8B / 70B (two sizes of one family) | tests H3 (scale) holding tokenizer/pretraining family constant |
| Mid-scale | Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct (or Mistral-Large) | cross-family replication |
| Frontier-class | GPT-4-class / Claude-class API model | ceiling behavior; also most likely to abstain rather than confabulate |

**Total probe count:** 200 pairs × 2 directions × 2 wording variants (gendered/neutral) × 2 templates (canonical + paraphrase, as a template-artifact guard) = **1,600 probes per model** (single run per probe; temperature 0 makes repeats unnecessary, and a 5% random rerun subset checks determinism).

---

## 4. Probes and scoring

### 4.1 Probe templates (examples)
- Forward, gendered: "Q: Who is the father of the actor {C full name}? A:"
- Reverse, gendered: "Q: Who is a son of the actor {P full name}? A:"
- Neutral variants replace father/mother → parent, son/daughter → child.
- Paraphrase variants: "…Name the {relation} of {entity}." / "…{Entity}'s {relation} is named…"

### 4.2 Response classification (per probe)
Each response is classified by deterministic rules over the alias tables, with a blind second-pass adjudicator (a human or a judge LLM *not in the panel*) resolving the residual cases:
- **CORRECT:** returned entity resolves to the ground-truth target via alias table.
- **ABSTENTION:** explicit refusal/uncertainty ("I don't know", "I'm not sure", refusal phrasing).
- **CONFABULATION:** a specific wrong named person (or a wrong-type answer, e.g., answering a spouse for "who is the parent").
- **INVALID:** off-topic, unparseable, or truncated nonsense.

**Primary metric:** CORRECT rate per direction.
**Secondary metrics:** abstention rate, confabulation rate, and a graded score (exact canonical match = 1, alias match = 0.75, correct first name only = 0.25) for sensitivity.

### 4.3 One-to-many parent→child scoring (stated primary convention)
Parent→child is intrinsically many-to-one. **Primary convention: a response naming any true child is CORRECT**, with a fixed enumeration budget — a response may list up to 3 named children; correct if ≥1 is true and none are asserted as the *only* child in a way that contradicts ground truth. Names outside the budget (listing >3) are still classified per rule but flagged.
**Robustness check:** restrict the analysis to the subset of parents with exactly one notable child (expected ~60–80 pairs) and re-estimate the direction gap. If the gap persists in the single-child subset, it cannot be an artifact of the enumeration convention.
Symmetrically, child→parent probes use "parent (mother/father)" so that either parent satisfies a gendered probe only when the wording matches the true relation; mismatched-wording responses are scored as wrong (the wording is chosen to match the true relation for that pair, so this is well-defined).

### 4.4 Multiple-choice sensitivity check
A constrained variant presents 4 options (1 true target, 3 same-relation distractors matched on salience and surname-overlap absence) for a random 50-pair subsample, both directions. This separates *recall failure* from *recognition failure*; a direction gap that vanishes under recognition suggests the deficit is in generation, not knowledge storage.

---

## 5. Statistical analysis plan

- **Primary test:** within-pair paired comparison of CORRECT/incorrect across directions — exact McNemar test on the 2×2 discordancy table, pooled over wording variants (after confirming no direction×wording interaction).
- **Power (feasibility check actually run during design):** Monte-Carlo simulation of the McNemar z-test, α = .05 two-sided, assuming discordance rate π_d ∈ {0.2, 0.3, 0.4} and P(forward correct | discordant) ∈ {0.70, 0.75}:
  - N=150: power 0.78–0.94 (gaps 10–16 pp)
  - N=200: power 0.88–0.98
  - N=250–300: power ≥0.94 in all scenarios
  **Conclusion:** N = 200 primary pairs is sufficient; the 150–300 range requested is feasible, with ~200 as the operating point. (These simulations justify the design size; they are not experimental results.)
- **Model:** mixed-effects logistic regression on per-probe correctness: direction (forward/reverse) as fixed effect of interest; covariates: salience stratum, target-side salience, wording variant, template, model; random intercepts for pair and model, random slope for direction by model (so the gap's cross-model consistency is estimated directly).
- **Effect-size call:** the bias is declared "present" if the direction gap is ≥10 pp, same sign, in ≥4 of 5 panel slots, with a significant pooled McNemar test.
- **H2 analysis:** among reverse-direction errors, test confabulation share > 50% (binomial test), and compare with forward-direction error composition.
- **Multiplicity:** the primary endpoint is single (direction gap on CORRECT rate); all other analyses are labeled secondary/exploratory.

---

## 6. Controls (summary)

1. **Direction pairing on identical triples** — every pair is its own control; paired statistics throughout.
2. **Salience balancing** — prompt-side entity is literally the same entity in both directions; target-side salience matched/recorded and modeled as covariate; stratified reporting.
3. **Name-ambiguity handling** — pre-registered exclusion rule, uniform role-hint disambiguation, blind alias tables.
4. **Leakage/contamination** — pre-2022 verifiability for all included facts; reference-density stratum; both directions co-occur in the same sources by construction.
5. **Wording & format symmetry** — gendered/neutral counterbalance, two templates, fixed answer slot, randomized probe order.
6. **Scoring convention symmetry** — same classifier and alias machinery for both directions; adjudicator blind to direction.
7. **Determinism checks** — 5% rerun subset; any nondeterminism absorbed by reporting majority-of-3 for flagged probes.

---

## 7. Feasibility and deliverable

- **Construction cost:** building 200 verified pairs with alias tables and salience scores is estimated at ~2–4 person-days using Wikidata dumps/SPARQL plus spot-checking; the most labor-intensive step is ambiguity screening.
- **Execution cost:** 1,600 probes × 5 model slots = 8,000 generations, trivially feasible for API or single-GPU local inference.
- **Optional artifact:** a runnable pipeline (probe generator, response classifier, analysis scripts) can accompany the design; the design document is complete and executable-by-others without it.
- **Known design limitations (stated, not fatal):** (a) "celebrity" salience proxies are imperfect; (b) pre-2022 famous relationships may be unequally represented in training corpora by individual, partially handled by the reference-density stratum; (c) frontier models may abstain more, compressing the CORRECT-rate gap — hence the joint reporting of abstention vs. confabulation composition, which is itself informative about the mechanism.

---

**Compliance notes:** No experiment was run; the only executed steps were workspace inspection (single file, `task.json`, containing the question; no datasets or materials present) and the §5 power simulation, which is a design-justification calculation, not an experimental result. All stated conventions (biological-relation default, pre-2022 cutoff, any-true-child-with-budget-3 scoring, N=200) are fixed and applied consistently as directed.

No datasets, seed entity lists, prior notes, or tooling are present. Nothing else relevant to the design was found.

**High-level design sketch**

1. *Task set construction.* Build a balanced parent↔child probe set over real-world celebrity family relationships. Each entity pair (parent P, child C) contributes two probes in a matched format:
   - Forward (child→parent): "Who is {C}'s parent/father/mother?" — expected answer: P.
   - Reverse (parent→child): "Who is {P}'s child/son/daughter?" — expected answer: C.
   Every pair thus serves as its own paired control, isolating direction while holding the factual triple constant.

2. *Candidate LLMs and prompting.* Evaluate a small panel of openly documented instruction-tuned models across scales (e.g., 2–4 families: one small ~7B, one mid ~30–70B, one frontier-class API model, and ideally one model family spanning multiple sizes to test scale effects). Use zero-shot free-form completion with a fixed template, temperature 0, plus one paraphrased template per direction to guard against template-specific artifacts. Optionally include a constrained multiple-choice variant as a sensitivity check (free-form recall vs. recognition).

3. *Scoring "accuracy."* Primary metric: exact-match / canonical-name match of the returned entity against the ground-truth target, after normalization (case, diacritics, honorifics, "the {parent} of X" phrasing). Secondary metrics: (a) acceptable-variant matching (aliases, full vs. stage names) judged by a deterministic alias table; (b) abstention rate ("I don't know") and confabulation rate (a *wrong named person* returned) — key because reverse-direction failures may manifest as hallucinated children rather than abstentions, which is itself part of the hypothesized phenomenon.

4. *Key controls.*
   - **Direction pairing:** identical entity pairs across both directions; analysis is within-pair (e.g., paired comparison / McNemar-style test on per-pair correct/incorrect), not across independent samples.
   - **Difficulty/celebrity-salience balancing:** stratify pairs by the prominence of each endpoint (e.g., quantified via a salience proxy such as Wikipedia pageviews or presence in a pre-2023 reference corpus). Match the two directions on the *prompt-side* entity's salience so the reverse direction isn't harder simply because parents queried are less famous (or more famous) than children queried. Report per-stratum results.
   - **Name-ambiguity handling:** prompt-side names must be unambiguous — disambiguate with a role hint (e.g., "the actor...") and exclude children/parents whose names collide with other highly salient celebrities; record any pair dropped for ambiguity.
   - **Leakage/contamination:** prefer relationships verifiable in sources predating the models' training cutoffs; document each pair's source and date; flag pairs likely inside training data vs. borderline; note that both directions of a famous fact are usually co-mentioned in the same documents, so co-occurrence is controlled by design — the test is about *retrieval direction*, not presence in training data.
   - **One-child vs. many-children asymmetry:** parent→child is intrinsically many-to-one; either (a) restrict to pairs where the parent has exactly one (notable) child, or (b) score any true child as correct with a fixed enumeration budget, and report both conventions as a robustness check.
   - **Gendered-role neutralization:** use gender-matched relation words (mother/father, son/daughter) or neutral "parent/child" wording, counterbalanced, to avoid wording asymmetry.
   - **Position/format effects:** keep answer slot and format identical across directions; randomize probe order.

5. *Analysis plan.* Primary endpoint: difference in accuracy between child→parent and parent→child directions, tested within-pair with a paired test and a mixed-effects logistic regression (direction, salience stratum, model family, template as covariates; pair and model as random effects). Predefine an effect-size threshold (e.g., ≥10 percentage-point gap consistently across models) for calling the bias "present."

## 1. Research question and hypothesis

**H1 (directional bias):** When queried about a real-world celebrity parent–child relationship, LLMs retrieve the **parent given the child** (child→parent, "forward") more accurately than the **child given the parent** (parent→child, "reverse"), measured within the same entity pair.

- H2: The reverse-direction deficit manifests disproportionately as *confabulation* (a confidently returned wrong child) rather than *abstention* ("I don't know"), because autoregressive completion of "X's child is ___" plausibly continues toward some plausible name.

## 2. Task set construction

### 2.1 Source and unit
- **Ground truth:** Wikipedia/Wikidata-sourced parent–child relations ("child" / "parent" / "father" / "mother" property statements), cross-checked against a second source (e.g., reputable biography or entertainment reference) for each included pair.
- **Unit of analysis:** one entity triple (Parent P, Child C, relation type), where **both P and C are individually Wikipedia-notable** with standalone articles. The famous-parent/less-notable-child case is **not excluded**; it forms one explicit salience stratification cell (§2.4).

### 2.2 Adjudication rule for blended/adoptive families (stated convention)
- **Primary dataset (default): biological relations only.** Include a pair only if the biological (or, for gestational surrogacy cases, the documented biological link) parent–child relation is stated in both sources. Adoptive and step relations are excluded from the primary set.
- **Robustness set:** a small supplementary subset (~30 pairs) of well-documented adoptive/step relations, analyzed separately and never pooled with the primary set. This isolates whether the direction effect differs for relations likely phrased differently in training text.

### 2.3 Ambiguity and name handling
- **Prompt-side uniqueness:** each probe names exactly one entity. A pair is excluded from the primary set if the prompt-side name collides with (a) another celebrity of comparable or higher salience with the same name, or (b) any entity plausibly confusable in the family domain. Disambiguating role hints ("the American actor…") are used uniformly in both directions, so hints do not differentially favor one direction.
- **Answer-side alias table:** for scoring, each entity has a canonical name plus an alias set (stage names, full legal names, common misspellings, e.g., "Coco" Arquette). The alias table is built once, blind to model outputs, from the same sources as ground truth.
- **Counterbalanced relation wording:** each pair appears in two template variants — gendered (mother/father, son/daughter, matched to the true relation) and neutral ("parent", "child") — counterbalanced for order, so wording asymmetry cannot masquerade as direction asymmetry.

### 2.4 Salience stratification (difficulty balancing between directions)
Each entity gets a salience score S (primary proxy: mean log10 Wikipedia pageviews over a fixed 12-month window; fallback proxy: article length percentile, pre-specified in case pageview data cannot be obtained offline). For each pair, record S_prompt(entity being asked about) and S_answer(target entity). Stratify pairs into 3 cells:
1. High–High (both endpoints S in top tercile)
2. Mixed (one endpoint top tercile, one bottom tercile) — this cell is further split by *which* endpoint is famous, giving four direction-salience combinations
3. Low–Low / famous-parent-obscure-child cell (includes the researcher-sanctioned famous-parent/notable-but-lesser-known-child case, kept as a labeled cell rather than excluded)

**Critical balance constraint:** within each salience cell, the distribution of S for the *prompt-side* entity must be matched across the two directions. That is, when comparing "who is C's parent" vs. "who is P's child," the entity named in the question is matched on salience across directions by construction (it is literally the same entity in the pair), and the *target-side* salience is recorded as a covariate so that "easier-to-name target" cannot confound the direction effect.

### 2.5 Contamination / cutoff policy (stated convention)
- **Inclusion rule:** every included pair must be verifiable in sources dated **before 2022-01-01**, which predates the training cutoff of every model in the panel. This makes the whole primary set "likely-in-training" and removes date as a confound between models.
- **Secondary stratification:** record for each pair a "reference density" indicator (number of pre-2022 sources stating the relation: 1 vs. ≥3). Pairs stated in only one marginal source are flagged *borderline* and analyzed as a stratum. No post-cutoff facts are included, so no unfair negatives exist.
- Note: both directions of a given fact typically co-occur in the same source documents; co-occurrence is thus constant within pair by design — the test isolates *retrieval direction*, not training-data presence.

### 2.6 Size
Target **N = 200 primary pairs** (acceptable operating range 150–300), allocated roughly evenly across salience cells. Justification in §5.

All models evaluated zero-shot, greedy decoding (temperature 0), identical system prompt, max completion length 64 tokens. Panel (as specified by the researcher; named here as concrete exemplars of each class — final names may be swapped for whatever is available at execution time, with the class structure preserved):

## 4. Probes and scoring

### 4.1 Probe templates (examples)
- Forward, gendered: "Q: Who is the father of the actor {C full name}? A:"
- Reverse, gendered: "Q: Who is a son of the actor {P full name}? A:"
- Neutral variants replace father/mother → parent, son/daughter → child.
- Paraphrase variants: "…Name the {relation} of {entity}." / "…{Entity}'s {relation} is named…"

### 4.2 Response classification (per probe)
Each response is classified by deterministic rules over the alias tables, with a blind second-pass adjudicator (a human or a judge LLM *not in the panel*) resolving the residual cases:
- **CORRECT:** returned entity resolves to the ground-truth target via alias table.
- **ABSTENTION:** explicit refusal/uncertainty ("I don't know", "I'm not sure", refusal phrasing).
- **CONFABULATION:** a specific wrong named person (or a wrong-type answer, e.g., answering a spouse for "who is the parent").
- **INVALID:** off-topic, unparseable, or truncated nonsense.

**Primary metric:** CORRECT rate per direction.
**Secondary metrics:** abstention rate, confabulation rate, and a graded score (exact canonical match = 1, alias match = 0.75, correct first name only = 0.25) for sensitivity.

### 4.3 One-to-many parent→child scoring (stated primary convention)
Parent→child is intrinsically many-to-one. **Primary convention: a response naming any true child is CORRECT**, with a fixed enumeration budget — a response may list up to 3 named children; correct if ≥1 is true and none are asserted as the *only* child in a way that contradicts ground truth. Names outside the budget (listing >3) are still classified per rule but flagged.
**Robustness check:** restrict the analysis to the subset of parents with exactly one notable child (expected ~60–80 pairs) and re-estimate the direction gap. If the gap persists in the single-child subset, it cannot be an artifact of the enumeration convention.
Symmetrically, child→parent probes use "parent (mother/father)" so that either parent satisfies a gendered probe only when the wording matches the true relation; mismatched-wording responses are scored as wrong (the wording is chosen to match the true relation for that pair, so this is well-defined).

### 4.4 Multiple-choice sensitivity check
A constrained variant presents 4 options (1 true target, 3 same-relation distractors matched on salience and surname-overlap absence) for a random 50-pair subsample, both directions. This separates *recall failure* from *recognition failure*; a direction gap that vanishes under recognition suggests the deficit is in generation, not knowledge storage.

## 5. Statistical analysis plan

- **Primary test:** within-pair paired comparison of CORRECT/incorrect across directions — exact McNemar test on the 2×2 discordancy table, pooled over wording variants (after confirming no direction×wording interaction).
- **Power (feasibility check actually run during design):** Monte-Carlo simulation of the McNemar z-test, α = .05 two-sided, assuming discordance rate π_d ∈ {0.2, 0.3, 0.4} and P(forward correct | discordant) ∈ {0.70, 0.75}:
  - N=150: power 0.78–0.94 (gaps 10–16 pp)
  - N=200: power 0.88–0.98
  - N=250–300: power ≥0.94 in all scenarios
  **Conclusion:** N = 200 primary pairs is sufficient; the 150–300 range requested is feasible, with ~200 as the operating point. (These simulations justify the design size; they are not experimental results.)
- **Model:** mixed-effects logistic regression on per-probe correctness: direction (forward/reverse) as fixed effect of interest; covariates: salience stratum, target-side salience, wording variant, template, model; random intercepts for pair and model, random slope for direction by model (so the gap's cross-model consistency is estimated directly).
- **Effect-size call:** the bias is declared "present" if the direction gap is ≥10 pp, same sign, in ≥4 of 5 panel slots, with a significant pooled McNemar test.
- **H2 analysis:** among reverse-direction errors, test confabulation share > 50% (binomial test), and compare with forward-direction error composition.
- **Multiplicity:** the primary endpoint is single (direction gap on CORRECT rate); all other analyses are labeled secondary/exploratory.

---

## 6. Controls (summary)

1. **Direction pairing on identical triples** — every pair is its own control; paired statistics throughout.
2. **Salience balancing** — prompt-side entity is literally the same entity in both directions; target-side salience matched/recorded and modeled as covariate; stratified reporting.
3. **Name-ambiguity handling** — pre-registered exclusion rule, uniform role-hint disambiguation, blind alias tables.
4. **Leakage/contamination** — pre-2022 verifiability for all included facts; reference-density stratum; both directions co-occur in the same sources by construction.
5. **Wording & format symmetry** — gendered/neutral counterbalance, two templates, fixed answer slot, randomized probe order.
6. **Scoring convention symmetry** — same classifier and alias machinery for both directions; adjudicator blind to direction.
7. **Determinism checks** — 5% rerun subset; any nondeterminism absorbed by reporting majority-of-3 for flagged probes.

---

## 7. Feasibility and deliverable

- **Construction cost:** building 200 verified pairs with alias tables and salience scores is estimated at ~2–4 person-days using Wikidata dumps/SPARQL plus spot-checking; the most labor-intensive step is ambiguity screening.
- **Execution cost:** 1,600 probes × 5 model slots = 8,000 generations, trivially feasible for API or single-GPU local inference.
- **Optional artifact:** a runnable pipeline (probe generator, response classifier, analysis scripts) can accompany the design; the design document is complete and executable-by-others without it.
- **Known design limitations (stated, not fatal):** (a) "celebrity" salience proxies are imperfect; (b) pre-2022 famous relationships may be unequally represented in training corpora by individual, partially handled by the reference-density stratum; (c) frontier models may abstain more, compressing the CORRECT-rate gap — hence the joint reporting of abstention vs. confabulation composition, which is itself informative about the mechanism.

Research question and hypothesis\n\n**H1 (directional bias):** When queried about a real-world celebrity parent\u2013child relationship, LLMs retrieve the **parent given the child** (child\u2192parent, \"forward\") more accurately than the **child given the parent** (parent\u2192child, \"reverse\"), measured within the same entity pair.\n\n**H0:** Direction has no effect on accuracy for a fixed factual triple.\n\n**Secondary hypotheses:**\n- H2: The reverse-direction deficit manifests disproportionately as *confabulation* (a confidently returned wrong child) rather than *abstention* (\"I don't know\"), because autoregressive completion of \"X's child is ___\" plausibly continues toward some plausible name.\n- H3 (scale): the direction gap shrinks with model scale (tested within one model family at multiple sizes).\n\n---\n\n## 2. Task set construction\n\n### 2.1 Source and unit\n- **Ground truth:** Wikipedia/Wikidata-sourced parent\u2013child relations (\"child\" / \"parent\" / \"father\" / \"mother\" property statements), cross-checked against a second source (e.g., reputable biography or entertainment reference) for each included pair.\n- **Unit of analysis:** one entity triple (Parent P, Child C, relation type), where **both P and C are individually Wikipedia-notable** with standalone articles. The famous-parent/less-notable-child case is **not excluded**; it forms one explicit salience stratification cell (\u00a72.4).\n\n### 2.2 Adjudication rule for blended/adoptive families (stated convention)\n- **Primary dataset (default): biological relations only.** Include a pair only if the biological (or, for gestational surrogacy cases, the documented biological link) parent\u2013child relation is stated in both sources. Adoptive and step relations are excluded from the primary set.\n- **Robustness set:** a small supplementary subset (~30 pairs) of well-documented adoptive/step relations, analyzed separately and never pooled with the primary set. This isolates whether the direction effect differs for relations likely phrased differently in training text.\n\n### 2.3 Ambiguity and name handling\n- **Prompt-side uniqueness:** each probe names exactly one entity. A pair is excluded from the primary set if the prompt-side name collides with (a) another celebrity of comparable or higher salience with the same name, or (b) any entity plausibly confusable in the family domain. Disambiguating role hints (\"the American actor\u2026\") are used uniformly in both directions, so hints do not differentially favor one direction.\n- **Answer-side alias table:** for scoring, each entity has a canonical name plus an alias set (stage names, full legal names, common misspellings, e.g., \"Coco\" Arquette).
